items.reason: The repo's SAST gate was decoration — `continue-on-error: true` in sast.yml and absent from check:ci, while AGENTS.md, SECURITY.md and the constraint map all called it blocking — so nothing here could go red for a security finding; I closed the four findings behind that line (two SQL interpolations fixed by enumerating the statements, one allowlisted with a reason and a raised ceiling, and the decrypted BYOM key moved behind a lib seam so no route imports it), deleted the softening, added `npm run sast` to check:ci and the job to required-checks/branch-ruleset, proved it bites with a known-bad fixture in gate-bite, and added a blocking lockfile-provenance suite; SHA-pinning the Actions remains open because it needs the network.

lessons: In this repository the interesting security question is never 'is there a gate?' but 'can it fail?'. Four documents (AGENTS.md, SECURITY.md, .github/constraint-map.json, .github/required-checks.json) called the SAST gate blocking while one `continue-on-error: true` line and an omission from `check:ci` meant it could not stop anything. Grep every claimed-blocking gate for `continue-on-error` and check it is actually a stage of `check:ci` before believing the prose — and note that `.github/constraint-map.json` is the file that is SUPPOSED to answer this, so a wrong row there is the highest-value thing to fix.

A softening that is honestly labelled and explicitly temporary is the kind that survives longest: sast.yml carried a well-written paragraph saying exactly which three findings had to be fixed before the line came out, and the line outlived it by months while a fourth finding accumulated behind it. A temporary exception is worth more when it names the count it is absorbing, so the count can be ratcheted, than when it names the fix.

Adding a stage to `check:ci` here is never a one-line diff: `test-unit/constraint-map.test.mjs` (a rule must claim the stage), `test-unit/gate-remedy.test.mjs` (a CHAIN entry, in the same order, whose script calls printRemedy), `test-unit/gate-bite.test.mjs` (a known-bad fixture or a written exemption), `test-unit/gate-timings.test.mjs` and the fence census all bind to that chain. Read those five before proposing a new gate — and note that `scripts/agent-surface.mjs`'s unmapped-file ratchet only counts `src/`, so new files under `scripts/` and `test-unit/` are free.

The contract ledger's `comesOffWhen` fields are executable design advice, not decoration. `plaintext-key-in-route` said the exception comes off 'when validation moves behind a lib-side seam that takes the user and returns a verdict' and that 'a second route needing the plaintext key is the signal to do that, not to add a line here' — which was exactly the situation, and following it turned an allowlist entry into a ceiling of 0. Read the ceiling's `comesOffWhen` before adding an entry to the list it caps.

An offline lane can still verify a lot about this tree with grep alone: the SAST rule set is ten regexes, so each one can be re-run by hand over `src/` to establish, before promoting the gate, that it is actually green — 88 API routes minus 83 with a guard is exactly the 5 allowlisted ones, and 860 of 866 lockfile entries carrying sha512 integrity turned out to be the 6 `inBundle` packages. Establish the count first; a promotion made on a guess is what makes a gate get switched off again.
